ja: עלה כלו קמשונים וגו', ואחזה אנכי אשית לבי ראיתי לקחתי מוסר. רשדנא אללה ואיאך אלי סביל טאעתה בעזתה ורחמתה תעאלי.
en_candidate:
**The sixth**: that the humble's work for God is accepted with God, as He said: "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit" (Psalms 51:19); and his sin is swiftly forgiven when he repents of it, as He said: "Whoever confesses and forsakes shall obtain mercy" (Proverbs 28:13); and: "When they are humbled, you say: 'Rise up'; and the lowered of eyes He shall save" (Job 22:29).

These are ten roots from the roots of humility; from them the rest of the excellences of this lofty, elevated, exalted disposition that I have not mentioned in this gate may be made plain to you. Reflect on what I have called your attention to of them; set it before your eyes; persist in thinking about it; be eager to acquire it; tend it perpetually from your soul and your dispositions; take help in God (mighty and exalted) for it; ask Him for the gift of it from Him, and seek to be granted it from Him as a means of nearing to Him and drawing close before Him — perhaps He will make it easy for you and open for you a door and a path to it, as one of the excellent ones used to add at his prayer: "My God, guard my tongue from evil and my lips from speaking deceit" — and the rest. Beware the whisperings of your heart and caprice's deception of you in what would carry you to haughtiness, self-conceit, vanity, vainglory, the seeking of leadership, elevation, command, prohibition, and the spread of fame among people. The Wise One has said the aspect of moderation for people in this world, in his saying: "Two things I have asked of You; do not deny them to me before I die. Vanity and a word of falsehood remove far from me; poverty and wealth do not give to me; nourish me with my apportioned bread — lest I be filled and deny and say, 'Who is the Lord?' or lest I become impoverished and steal, and seize upon the name of my God" (Proverbs 30:7–9).

Wake up, O my brother! Do not be heedless of the treatment of this self-conceit from your soul and your dispositions, by the medicines I have pointed you to. Let it not prevent you from this, what you see upon the bulk of people of heedlessness in the treating of themselves of this disease — saying, "What is good enough for them is good enough for me." For the blind man, when there are present to him beneficial collyria by which his cure is possible at their use, it is not from prudence for him to delay this and say, "What is good enough for my blind companions is good enough for me." Were one of them to say to you this saying, you would consider his saying foolish, and his judgment incompetent, and would remove him from the rank of the rational. So in proportion to that, look to your soul, my brother; take it with prudence; do not be lazy in what would benefit you in your this-world and your next-world — lest you die without reaching your hopes in the excellences which are in your power to attain — as the Wise One said: "The desire of the sluggard kills him, for his hands refuse to do" (Proverbs 21:25); and he said: "I passed by the field of a sluggard and by the vineyard of a man lacking heart; and behold, it was all overgrown with thorns…  I beheld and set my heart upon it; I saw and received instruction" (Proverbs 24:30–32).

May God guide us and you to the path of His obedience, by His might and His mercy (exalted be He).
